corrected_value.authors: Opfer, J. E., & Siegler, R. S.
corrected_value.title: Representational change and children’s numerical estimation.

decision.quote: We used the same values as Opfer and Siegler, which allowed for better discrimination between logarithmic and linear representations. Positive values included 2, 5, 18, 34, 56, 78, 100, 122, 147,150, 163, 179, 246, 366, 486, 606, 722, 725, 738, 754, 818, and 938. Negative values were exactly the same but were presented with a negative sign. Given the variety of number estimation tasks that exist and the importance of the type of task for this skill (see Cohen & Sarnecka, 2014), we chose to use two separate lines (positive and negative) for two reasons. First, we wanted to directly replicate Siegler’s work (Opfer & Siegler, 2007)as closely as possible and thus chose to use the original positive number line and values used in those studies.
decision.reason: Prior adjudication and state files were checked and are absent for this never-adjudicated work. In the Method (p. 344) and Discussion (pp. 354–355), the authors explicitly state that they designed the positive 0–1,000 number-line task and 22 target values to directly replicate Opfer and Siegler (2007) as closely as possible and to provide a direct comparison to those findings, testing logarithmic versus linear estimation fits in 2nd, 4th, and 6th graders. The reference list (p. 357) establishes the original identity as Opfer, J. E., & Siegler, R. S. (2007), 'Representational change and children’s numerical estimation,' Cognitive Psychology, 55, 169–195 (no DOI printed in source). This 2007 Cognitive Psychology study is a separate independent work from shipped row 2447 (Siegler & Opfer, 2003, Psychological Science, 14, 237–243, 10.1111/1467-9280.02438) and from sibling target 0 (Booth & Siegler, 2006, Developmental Psychology, 41, 189–201), all three of which appear as distinct entries in the paper's reference list; report equivalence does not apply.
